title: Status and utility icons
instruction: Give each record state or interface action a glyph and a word that read without color.
intro: A glyph here is a small drawn mark, and each one carries its meaning twice, in its shape and in the word beside it. A reader who sees no color, or prints the page in gray, gets the same meaning as everyone else.

Trackers come first: they show how far a bill has come in six numbered steps, and the same marks then follow a records request or an agency rule. After them come the utility icons, which sit beside the word for an action on a page, and the three marks that give an error, a success or a warning its shape.

groups.title: Trackers
groups.line: A tracker shows where a bill stands in six numbered steps, with each step’s state drawn as a shape and said in words.

groups.title: Records requests and agency rules
groups.line: A request for public records and a federal agency’s rule each move through six steps of their own, drawn with the tracker’s marks.

groups.title: Utility icons
groups.line: A utility icon names an action on a page, such as Close, Download or Filter, beside the words that say it.

groups.title: Error, success and warning
groups.line: Three marks give a message its shape, and the words beside them say what happened and what to do.

rules.title: Follow every bill through six numbered steps with plain names.
rule: A tracker follows a bill through six steps, numbered 1 to 6: Filed, Hearing, Committee vote, First chamber, Second chamber, and a sixth named for whoever signs the bill, Governor on a state bill and President on a federal one. A chamber is one house of a legislature, such as the House or the Senate, and the first chamber is the one where the bill was filed. Every tracker prints the number and the name together, as in “Step 2 of 6: Hearing”, for the step the bill is at now.

Six steps fold some procedure together, such as a second reading or a conference committee, where members of both chambers settle one text. A bill’s own page gives those dates in the note under the step they belong to. Every state keeps all six steps. Nebraska’s Legislature has one chamber, so a Nebraska bill keeps step 5 under a slash, and its card says “Nebraska has one chamber” beside the marks.

text: A number gives a reader words to say, “step 2 of 6”, with no key to learn, and it reads the same on a phone and in gray print. Plain names let a newcomer say what happens at each step. The hearing keeps a step of its own because it is where a committee takes testimony on the bill, from the public in many state legislatures and from the witnesses it invites in Congress. Naming step 6 for the person who signs keeps a bill that waits for a signature from reading as law.
why.basis: Design judgment, approved by our founder and editor in November 2026

correct.caption: Three bills at 360 px, each at step 6 with its own key. The state bill’s sixth step is Governor and the federal bill’s is President. The Nebraska bill keeps all six steps, with step 5 under a slash and the reason beside it.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 11.1. The steps take the clerk’s names. A newcomer cannot say what Engrossed or Enrolled means, so the tracker needs a glossary before it tells anyone where the bill stands.

specs.label: Steps
specs.value: 1 Filed, 2 Hearing, 3 Committee vote, 4 First chamber, 5 Second chamber, 6 the signer

specs.label: Step 6
specs.value: Governor on a state bill; President on a federal bill

specs.label: Nebraska
specs.value: Six steps; step 5 under a slash, with “Nebraska has one chamber” beside the marks

specs.label: Status words
specs.value: “Step 2 of 6: Hearing.”, in bold, for the step the bill is at now, then one plain sentence

specs.label: Step names under the circles
specs.value: In a list column 552 px wide or more, Inter 600 at 13 px, the current step in bold

builders: Write the status words from the data, never from the drawing: the step number, its name for this bill’s route and one sentence on what happens next. Store step 6 as the signer, so a state bill prints Governor and a federal bill prints President.

Number an invented bill past the numbers legislatures assign: a federal bill from H.R. 99001 up, state bills from one count that starts at H.99001 and S.99002, and a Nebraska bill with Nebraska’s LB, for Legislative Bill, from LB 99008 up. Label each one Illustrative. A cropped plate then cannot put our status words on a real bill.

rules.title: Draw each step’s state as a shape, and say it in words.
rule: Each step shows its state by its shape, and the words beside the tracker say the same thing. Done steps fill in, the step a bill is at now takes a heavy ring, and steps ahead keep a fine one. A step that never happened, such as a hearing the committee skipped, keeps its number under a slash, so the count still runs to six. When a bill stops, its line ends on a filled square at that step.

text: A shape holds up in gray print, in bright sun and for the many readers who cannot tell red from green. The words carry the state to a screen reader and to anyone unsure of a mark. Every mark a bill has reached draws in the surface’s ink, Charcoal on Newsprint and Newsprint on Charcoal, as do the slash and the line up to the current step. The rings ahead, the ring under a slash and the line after the current step draw lighter, in Stone on Newsprint and Dim Newsprint on Charcoal, so the steps still to come stand back. Only the take-part disc is red.

correct.caption: The six states, each drawn on step 4 at true size. Each one changes the shape, so the set reads in grayscale.

failure.caption: Fails WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1. Six identical circles tell their states by hue alone. In grayscale, the done steps in Verdigris and the steps ahead in Stone print as grays 1.25 to 1 apart, and no word says where the bill stands.

specs.label: Done
specs.value: A filled circle, its number in the surface color

specs.label: Now
specs.value: A ring with a 3 px line, its number in bold

specs.label: Not yet
specs.value: A ring with a 1.5 px line in Stone, its number in Inter 600 in the secondary text color

specs.label: Never happened
specs.value: The Not yet ring under a 2 px slash in ink, 4 px longer than the circle is wide

specs.label: Halo
specs.value: A 4 px stroke in the surface color under the number of a step that never happened, which shows 2 px around it

specs.label: Stopped
specs.value: A filled square 2 px narrower than the circle, in its place; the line ends there

specs.label: Marks on Newsprint
specs.value: Charcoal 13.29 to 1, Stone 4.29 to 1

specs.label: Marks on Charcoal
specs.value: Newsprint 13.29 to 1, Dim Newsprint 7.26 to 1

specs.label: Numbers ahead
specs.value: Deep Stone 5.49 to 1 on Newsprint, Dim Newsprint 7.26 to 1 on Charcoal

builders: Draw each tracker as one SVG with aria-hidden="true", and give screen readers an ordered list of the six steps beside it, each with its state in words, such as “Step 2, Hearing: never happened.” Hide that list visually and keep it in the reading order.
Tag each mark data-icon="S-now" (or S-done, S-take-part, S-not-yet, S-never-happened, S-stopped) with data-icon-family="status", so the shared checks find it.
A hearing on the bill’s subject held before the bill was filed does not fill step 2; the step’s note names it.
Draw each mark from the table after this rule, Drawing the marks, which gives its size at every circle size, its line, its color token and where its parts sit.

rules.title: Say in words when a bill becomes law or stops.
rule: Step 6 keeps the signer’s name while a bill waits, so a bill there reads “Step 6 of 6: Governor”. Once it becomes law, all six steps fill and the words say “Became law on” with the date, then when it takes effect, as in “Became law on April 2. It takes effect July 1.” A bill can become law by signature, by a vote to override a veto, or without a signature where the constitution allows it. When it was not signed, the words say how, as in “Became law on March 18, over the governor’s veto.”
A bill that stops ends its line on a square at the step where it stopped, and the words give the date and the reason. A veto that stands stops a bill at step 6.

text: A reader who sees the last step filled can take the bill for law, so only the words can say when the signature came and when the law applies. The date it takes effect is the one most readers act on.
why.basis: Design judgment, approved by our founder and editor in November 2026

correct.caption: Three ends at 360 px. H.99003 became law when it was signed, and S.99006 over a veto; the words of each say how and when. S.99005 stopped at step 6 when a veto stood, and its line ends on the square.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 11.3. The sixth step is named Law, so a bill that still waits for the governor reads “Step 6 of 6: Law.” A reader may stop following it before a veto.

specs.label: Waiting to be signed
specs.value: “Step 6 of 6: Governor.” or “Step 6 of 6: President.”

specs.label: Signed
specs.value: All six steps filled; “Became law on April 2. It takes effect July 1.”

specs.label: Over a veto
specs.value: All six steps filled; “Became law on March 18, over the governor’s veto.”

specs.label: Without a signature
specs.value: All six steps filled; “Became law on May 4, without the governor’s signature.”, where the constitution allows it

specs.label: Stopped
specs.value: A square at the last step reached; “Stopped at step 3 of 6: Committee vote.” with the date and the reason

specs.label: A veto that stands
specs.value: Stopped at step 6

builders: Keep two dates in a bill’s record once it is signed: the day it was signed and the day it takes effect, written in the past tense once that day has passed. Print “Became law on” only from the signed date.

rules.title: Mark the one way to take part in red, on its own shape, beside its words.
rule: When the public can act on a bill before a date, the step it is at takes the take-part mark: a small red disc at the upper right of its ring, with a 1 px Charcoal keyline inside the disc’s edge. The words “You can take part now” sit beside it, with the deadline and the way to act. It is the view’s one working red (Rule 05.3), and it can sit on any step where the public can take part, such as a hearing in the second chamber at step 5. Every other state stays in the surface’s ink.

text: Red catches the eye first, so it goes to the one thing a reader can do. The disc changes the ring’s outline, so the mark still reads in gray print, and the words say what to do for anyone who cannot see red. On Newsprint, Pillar Red measures 2.96 to 1, under the 3 to 1 a mark needs, and the keyline gives it an edge at 13.29 to 1.

correct.caption: A story card at 360 px. The House committee holds its own hearing at step 5, so the take-part mark sits there, beside its words and the link to act.

failure.caption: Fails Rules 11.4 and 05.3. Red also fills the steps the bill has passed, so it does two jobs and the one way to take part no longer stands out.

specs.label: Take-part mark
specs.value: An 11 px Pillar Red disc at the upper right of the Now ring, a 1 px Charcoal keyline inside its edge, 1.5 px of the surface around it

specs.label: Contrast
specs.value: Pillar Red 2.96 to 1 on Newsprint with the keyline at 13.29; 4.49 to 1 on Charcoal

specs.label: Words
specs.value: “You can take part now.” in bold, then the deadline and how to act

specs.label: In a list, or on a card with this mark
specs.value: A text link at least 44 px tall; the red button waits for the bill’s own page

specs.label: On a card without this mark
specs.value: The card may end on the red ask, as the pillar cards in chapter 01 do

specs.label: Red jobs in a view
specs.value: One: take part now. Every take-part mark and the ask button share it. An error in the same view takes the red first (Rule 11.16)

builders: Mark the disc and the ask button with data-red="working" and data-red-job="take part now", so the shared check counts one red job. The words carry the meaning, so the disc stays hidden from screen readers.

rules.title: Use numbered steps in lists and on story cards.
rule: In a list of bills and on a story card, the tracker runs across the page: six numbered circles on one line, solid as far as the bill has come and fine after it. The bill’s number and name lead each row, and its status words follow the marks. In a column narrower than 552 px, as on a phone, the first circle starts on the text edge and the step names move into a key after the list. In a wider column, each step takes a sixth of the row and its name sits under its circle.

text: A list asks a reader to compare bills at a glance, and six numbered steps fit across a 360 px phone with room for the words. The numbers also keep the tracker apart from the lockmark, the small grid of lines and nodes that marks our pages and codes nothing (chapter 08).
why.basis: Design judgment, approved by our founder and editor in November 2026

correct.caption: Five bills at 360 px on Newsprint, among them one where you can take part, one waiting for the governor, one whose hearing never happened and one stopped by a veto.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 11.5. Dots on a line carry no numbers or names, so a reader counts dots to find the step, and a row of nodes on a line comes close to the lockmark’s drawing.

specs.label: Circles
specs.value: 26 px in a phone list, 30 px in a wide list, 24 px on a story card

specs.label: Line
specs.value: 2 px in the surface’s ink as far as the record has come, through any step that never happened; 1 px in Stone after the current step

specs.label: Spacing
specs.value: Phone list and card: the first circle on the text edge and each next one 60 px on, center to center, so six fit a 328 px row. Wide list: one sixth of a 552 px row to each step, 92 px

specs.label: Key

builders: Mark up the list as a <ul> of bills, each holding its hidden step list from Rule 11.2. Switch to the wide form with a container query on the list’s own width, @container (min-width: 34.5rem), so a list in a narrow column keeps its key at any window size. When a tracker updates in place, announce the new status words through a polite live region, as chapter 18 sets out.

rules.title: Turn the same steps upright on a bill’s own page.
rule: A bill’s own page runs the six steps down the page, with the marks a list uses. Each step gives its name, its state in words and a note with its dates. Under the step where the public can act, a box holds the deadline and the page’s one red button, the ask. Where the page has room, a key after the steps says what each one means.

text: A bill’s page has room for the dates and notes a list leaves out, and a reader who knows the marks from a list knows them here. The ask sits under the step it belongs to, where the reader learns why the date matters.
why.basis: Design judgment, approved by our founder and editor in November 2026

correct.caption: H.99001’s page at 360 px. Step 2 holds the way to take part, and step 5’s note says the Senate’s committee often holds a hearing of its own.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 11.6. A generic stepper from a component library draws checks and boxes with no numbers, so a reader who learned the steps in a list has to learn a second set.

specs.label: Circles
specs.value: 28 px with 14 px numbers

specs.label: Line

rules.title: Size the marks for reading, and the targets for a thumb.
rule: Draw the circles at 24 px on a story card, 26 px in a phone list, 28 px on a bill’s page and 30 px in a wide list. Numbers sit at 13 px in circles under 28 px and at 14 px from 28 px.

Every link and button in a tracker, and every control that carries a utility icon, stands at least 44 px tall, and the ask button 48 px. A plain list of text links, such as a list of contents, may stand shorter, as long as each link keeps the 24 px that WCAG asks for through its spacing.

text: Numbers at 13 px keep the type floor of Rule 06.3 inside the mark. A target 44 px tall clears the 24 px minimum in WCAG 2.2 with room for a thumb, and matches our touch target token.

correct.caption: The four circle sizes at true size, and the two targets with their heights marked.

failure.caption: Fails Rules 11.7 and 06.3. Circles at 16 px force numbers down to 9 px, and the link stands 20 px tall, under the 24 px minimum.

specs.label: Circles
specs.value: 24, 26, 28 and 30 px, by place

specs.label: Numbers

specs.label: Links and buttons in a tracker, and controls with a utility icon

rules.title: Follow a records request through six steps, and end it in plain words.
rule: A records request asks a government agency to release documents it holds. These steps and end words follow the federal Freedom of Information Act and the Justice Department’s categories; a request to a state or local agency follows that state’s law. The tracker uses the bill tracker’s marks for six steps of its own: Requested, Acknowledged, Searching, Reviewing, Answered and Appeal. Step 6 counts only when the requester appeals, so a request that was never appealed keeps step 6 under a slash once the time to appeal has passed.

The words say how the agency answered, with the date: Granted, Partly granted, Denied, or Closed with no records released. A request the requester stopped reads “Withdrawn by the requester”, and its line ends on a square at the step where it stopped. An appeal ends in words too: Upheld, Partly reversed, Reversed and sent back, or Closed for other reasons.

text: A requester can wait weeks for an answer, and the steps tell them where the request sits. The marks are the bill tracker’s, so a reader learns them once. The end words follow the Justice Department’s own categories in plain words, with one change: the department counts a withdrawn request among its denials, and a reader who saw “denied” would think the agency had refused.

correct.caption: Three requests at 360 px. One is under review, one was partly granted and never appealed, so step 6 keeps its slash, and one was withdrawn at step 3.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 11.8. The tracker prints the government’s category for a request the requester withdrew, so “Full denial” tells a reader the agency refused.

specs.label: Steps
specs.value: 1 Requested, 2 Acknowledged, 3 Searching, 4 Reviewing, 5 Answered, 6 Appeal

specs.label: Step 6
specs.value: A fine ring while an appeal can still be filed; under a slash once the time has passed with none

specs.label: The answer, in words
specs.value: Granted; Partly granted; Denied; Closed, no records released; Withdrawn by the requester

specs.label: An appeal, in words
specs.value: Upheld; Partly reversed; Reversed and sent back; Closed for other reasons

specs.label: Marks and sizes
specs.value: The bill tracker’s, from Rules 11.2 and 11.7

builders: Store each request’s step and its end words as data, and print the end words with their date: “Partly granted on March 3.” A state’s records law sets its own deadlines, so check that state’s statute before you print one. Number an invented request from 99001 up, name no agency, and label it Illustrative.

rules.title: Follow an agency rule through six steps, and mark the open comment period as the way to take part.
rule: A federal agency writes a rule in six steps: Early notice, Proposed, Comments open, Comments closed, Final rule and In effect. Step 1 is optional, so a rule that had no early notice keeps step 1 under a slash. While comments are open, step 3 takes the take-part mark from Rule 11.4, with the deadline and how to send a comment.

A rule the agency issued without asking for comment first keeps steps 2 to 4 under slashes, and its words say so: “Issued without advance comment.” An interim final rule is one such rule, and it takes comments only after it takes effect. A rule that ends early says how in words, with the date: Withdrawn by the agency, Struck by Congress, or Set aside by a court. Once a rule takes effect, all six steps fill, as a bill’s do once it becomes law.

text: Sending a comment is the main way the law gives the public to take part in a federal rule, so the open comment period carries the view’s working red, as a hearing does on a bill. The slashes keep a rule that skipped comment from reading as one the public had a say in before it took effect.

correct.caption: Three agency rules at 360 px. Comments are open on one, so step 3 takes the take-part mark; one took effect without advance comment, with slashes on steps 1 to 4; and one was withdrawn after comments closed.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 11.9. Steps 2 to 4 are filled for a rule issued without advance comment, so the tracker tells a reader the public had its say before the rule took effect.

specs.label: Steps
specs.value: 1 Early notice, 2 Proposed, 3 Comments open, 4 Comments closed, 5 Final rule, 6 In effect

specs.label: Step 1
specs.value: Optional; under a slash when the agency gave no early notice

specs.label: Take part
specs.value: On step 3 while comments are open: the take-part mark, the deadline and “How to send a comment”

specs.label: Without advance comment
specs.value: Steps 2 to 4 under slashes, and “Issued without advance comment.”

specs.label: The end, in words
specs.value: In effect since; Withdrawn by the agency; Struck by Congress; Set aside by a court, with the part it set aside

specs.value: Usually 30 days or more after the final rule is published, and 60 days or more for a major rule

builders: Store the comment deadline with the rule, and take the take-part mark off the day comments close. Number an invented rule from 99001 up, name no agency, and label it Illustrative.

rules.title: Say a wait or a later step in words, and keep the count at six.
rule: A wait inside a step, such as an agency’s question to the requester, a fee estimate or an extension of up to 10 working days, shows as words under the step it falls in. It never adds a mark, so every request still counts to six. A step outside the agency, such as mediation by the National Archives or a lawsuit, follows the end words as a sentence with its date.

A status taken from the agency’s own tracking service, or from the Federal Register for a rule, needs no mark. A status we piece together ourselves, such as a wait we learn of from the agency’s letter, carries the warning mark and the date we checked it: “Checked April 20. The agency may have acted since.”

text: The law lets an agency stop its 20 working days while it waits on the requester, once for more information and again to settle fees, and add up to 10 working days in unusual circumstances, so each wait belongs inside the step it falls in. A count that changed from one request to the next would stop readers from comparing them. The check date tells a reader how old the status is before they rely on it.

correct.caption: Two requests at 360 px. One waits on the requester at step 3, in words, with the date we last checked it beside the warning mark. The other was upheld on appeal and then taken to court, said in a sentence after its end words.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 11.10. The fee estimate becomes a seventh step, so this request reads “Step 4 of 7” while every other request counts to six.

specs.label: Waits, in words
specs.value: “Waiting on you”, a fee estimate or an extension, under the step it falls in, with its date

specs.label: A proposed rule that sits
specs.value: “No action since” and the date, under its step

specs.label: After the agency
specs.value: Mediation or a lawsuit, in a sentence after the end words

specs.label: Check date

specs.label: Marks
specs.value: Six, always

rules.title: Set each utility icon beside its word, at 24 px by a control and 16 px only inside a line of text.
rule: A utility icon names an action on a page, such as Close, Download or Filter. It sits beside its word: 24 px wide beside the word of a button or link, and 16 px wide only inside a line of text or a table heading, where it comes from its own 16 px drawing. Three icons sit beside other words that carry their meaning: the sort mark beside a column’s heading, the mark after a link to another site and the chevron beside a row’s words. The clear control inside a search field is the one icon with no word; its field’s label gives the context, and its name is “Clear the search”.

Share, zoom, print and information stay words. Their usual signs repeat drawings we already use, such as the two rings of the Connect pillar icon and the atlas’s plus and minus, and an information mark invites help that shows only on hover.

text: A reader who meets an icon beside its word learns the sign once, and the word carries the meaning for anyone who does not know the sign. With the word showing, the icon stays hidden from screen readers, so nobody hears the action twice, and a control’s name starts with the words a reader sees, which voice control needs. A name that shows only on hover never reaches a phone, a keyboard or a magnified screen.

correct.caption: A report reader’s toolbar, live at 360 px. Each icon sits beside its word, every control stands 44 px tall, Previous page says why it is unavailable on the first page, and the control for the page’s size stays in words.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 11.11. The toolbar shows icons with no words, each 32 px square, and its information mark gives its name only in a box that appears on hover.

specs.label: Inside a line of text or a table heading
specs.value: The 16 px drawing, 1.5 px line, on the line with its word

specs.label: Control
specs.value: At least 44 px tall; 44 by 44 px where the icon stands with no word

Take a 16 px icon from svg-16/, and never scale the 24 px drawing down. An unavailable control keeps its focus, takes aria-disabled="true" and points with aria-describedby to words that say why.

rules.title: Give each drawing one meaning.
rule: The arrow means Next. Mirrored, it means Previous, and turned up or down it shows the order a column is sorted in. The chevron opens and closes a row: it points down while the row is closed and up while it is open. The cross closes, and an error is a circle holding an exclamation mark. Copy’s two sheets never turn into a check; the result goes to a status line in words, with the success or the error mark.
Menu’s three bars stay bars while the menu is open, and the open menu carries its own Close.

text: A reader learns a sign once and trusts it after that. If the chevron also turned pages, a reader could not tell a row that opens from a page that turns, and a Copy icon that turned into a check would look like a choice someone had made.

correct.caption: The symbol library’s search and filter bar, live at 360 px. The funnel opens the filters, the chevron shows they are open, a check marks the filter that is on, and the cross clears the search.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 11.12. The chevron turns the page in the toolbar and opens the sources below it, so one drawing does two jobs in one view.

specs.label: Cross

specs.label: Selected check
specs.value: Inside a chip that is on, before its word, with a heavier outline

specs.label: Copy

specs.label: Menu
specs.value: Three bars, open or closed; the open menu holds Close and the Escape key, and focus returns to Menu

builders: Turn and mirror the arrow and the chevron with the transforms in the utility manifest, on the <use>, so every line stays on the pixel grid. At 16 px the down arrow is a mirror across the diagonal, matrix(0 1 1 0 0 0), which keeps its shaft on the up arrow’s pixel column.

Give a search field type="search" and let the Escape key clear it. On a product page, wrap the field, its filters and its status line in a search landmark, the <search> element, so a screen reader can jump straight to it, as Rule 18.15’s code does. Write the count and any advice to that one status line, such as “0 of 125 symbols. No symbol matches. Clear the search or the filters to see more.” Rule 18.15 is the search’s home, with every state and its code to copy.

rules.title: Mark a link to another site, and open it in the same tab.
rule: A link that leaves our site opens in the same tab. Its mark, an arrow leaving a box, follows the link’s last word at 16 px and stays on the line with that word, and the words “(another site)” end the link’s name for screen readers. A link that must open a new tab says so instead: “(opens in a new tab)”.

text: A reader knows before pressing that the link leaves Oath & Action. A new tab that opens unannounced takes away the Back button and can strand a screen reader or magnifier user on a page they did not choose.

correct.caption: Three sources, live at 360 px. Each link opens in the same tab, its mark follows its last word, and each stands 44 px tall in the list.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 11.13. The link opens a new tab and says nothing about it, and its 24 px mark has broken from its word onto a line of its own.

specs.label: Mark
specs.value: Another site, 16 px, after the last word, in a span that does not wrap

specs.label: Hidden words
specs.value: “(another site)”, or “(opens in a new tab)” where it does

specs.label: Target
specs.value: In running text, the line, at least 24 px tall; in a list of sources, 44 px tall

builders: Wrap the last word and the mark in <span style="white-space: nowrap">, then the hidden words in a visually hidden span inside the link, so its name reads “... (another site)”. Leave out target="_blank".

rules.title: Keep topic and atlas symbols out of buttons, and draw each action with its utility icon.
rule: A topic or atlas symbol names a subject: a feedback loop, public records, a vote. It never stands for an action on a page. Reset is the utility icon’s open circle with one arrowhead, Download is the arrow into a tray, and each sits beside its word.

text: A symbol that works as a button in one place and names a subject in another teaches the reader two meanings for one drawing. CL-024, Feedback loop, looks most like a refresh sign, and a loop stepper is where a builder would reach for one.

correct.caption: A stepper for Loop R1 from our systems atlas, “Wealth and political influence reinforce each other”, live at 360 px. Play, Reset the loop, Previous step and Next step each carry a utility icon beside the word, and the unavailable ones say why. The least certain step says so in its words.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 11.14. CL-024, the feedback loop drawing, stands in for Reset. A reader learns it as a button here and meets it next as the subject of a story about feedback loops.

specs.label: Reset
specs.value: Three quarters of a circle with one arrowhead; “Reset” or “Start over” and its object

specs.label: Play and Pause
specs.value: One button: its icon and word change together; playback starts only on a press

specs.label: Pace
specs.value: Play holds each step about 250 ms a word and never under 6 seconds, with reduced motion too: 9 to 12.75 seconds a step here. Pause stops it, and Next step turns one step at a time

specs.label: Step words
specs.value: The verb follows the connection’s sign; a step graded plausible takes “can” and says its grade

specs.label: Topic and atlas symbols
specs.value: Beside their own word, never inside a button that does something (Rule 10.1)

builders: When a control needs an icon the utility set lacks, use the word alone and ask the editor, and leave chapter 10’s drawings to the subjects they name.

rules.title: Give each error, success and warning its mark and its words.
rule: An error, a success and a warning each take their mark before their words. The error mark is a circle holding an exclamation mark, in the text’s ink, on the pale Error Band with a 4 px red bar, and its words start “Error:” and say how to fix it. The success mark is a check leaving an open circle, in Verdigris, beside what happened. The warning mark is a triangle holding an exclamation mark, in ink, beside the notice, such as the date a record was last checked.

A field with an error carries the red bar at its left edge and points to its message, and focus moves to the first field to fix. Copy, Search, Filter and Sort write their results to a status line in words.

text: Each state has a shape and a word, so none rests on color. The error mark draws in ink because Pillar Red measures 2.64 to 1 on the Error Band and 2.96 on Newsprint, under the 3 to 1 a mark needs; in ink it measures 11.89 to 1, and the red bar carries the error’s claim on the view’s red. Verdigris measures 3.37 to 1 on Newsprint.

correct.caption: A sign-up form, live at 360 px. Send it with a field wrong to see the error mark, its words and the red bar, and the red button step down to Charcoal; send it right to see the success mark.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 11.15 and WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1. The message is red text beside a cross. The cross means Close, the red text measures 2.96 to 1, and nothing says “Error” or how to fix the entry.

specs.label: Error mark
specs.value: A circle holding an exclamation mark, in the text’s ink, never red

specs.label: The red bar
specs.value: 4 px of Pillar Red at the left of the message and of a field with an error; this token colors the bar only

specs.label: Error message
specs.value: On the Error Band: the mark, “Error:” and the fix

specs.label: Field with an error
specs.value: The red bar at its left edge, aria-invalid and aria-describedby to its message

specs.label: Success
specs.value: The mark in Verdigris, 3.37 to 1, beside what happened

specs.label: Warning
specs.value: The mark in ink, never red, with a 4 px bar in ink; never for an evidence grade or an Illustrative label

specs.label: Size
specs.value: 24 px beside a message; 16 px inside a line of text

builders: Put an error message in role="alert" or in a status line the field points to, and a success or a result in role="status". Draw the bar as a left border, which stays visible when the system forces its own colors.
Draw the error mark in --oa-color-state-error-text-on-newsprint through currentColor. --oa-color-state-error-mark-on-newsprint colors the 4 px bar only.

rules.title: When an error, the take-part mark and an intervention marker meet, give the error the red.
rule: Rule 05.3 gives each view one working red, in this order: an error the reader must fix, then the step a reader can take now, then the one point the headline names, which in a systems figure is where a reform acts. So when the three meet in one view, the error keeps the red. The take-part mark yields: its disc draws in the surface’s ink, keeps its place on the ring, and “You can take part now” stays beside it, while the ask button steps down to Charcoal. The intervention marker yields too: its outline stays heavier, in ink, with its words.
Once the reader fixes the error, the red goes back to the take-part mark and the ask. The intervention marker takes the red only in a view with no error and no step to take.

text: A reader has to fix an error before taking any step, and a step a reader can take matters more than a point we want to make. Each mark keeps its shape and its words when it yields, so nothing it says is lost.

correct.caption: One view at 360 px. The email field’s error holds the red. The take-part disc on step 2 and the heavier outline where reform R-32, public and philanthropic funding for local news, acts stay in Charcoal with their words, and Remind me is Charcoal until the error is fixed.

failure.caption: Fails Rules 11.16 and 05.3. The error, the take-part mark and the intervention marker all take red, so the error that blocks the reader looks no more urgent than the rest.

specs.label: First claim
specs.value: An error the reader must fix, which holds the red bar

specs.label: Error mark
specs.value: In the text’s ink, beside the red bar

specs.label: Second claim
specs.value: The step a reader can take now: the take-part mark and the ask

specs.label: Third claim
specs.value: Where a reform acts: the intervention marker

specs.label: A mark that yields
specs.value: Keeps its shape, its place and its words, in the surface’s ink

specs.label: The ask while an error shows
specs.value: Charcoal primary button

builders: Mark each red with data-red="working" and its data-red-job. When an error appears, move the red: draw the take-part disc and the marker in ink, swap the ask to --oa-component-button-primary-fill-on-newsprint, and swap them back once the error is gone.

extras.label: The six steps
extras.caption: What happens at each step. Step 6 takes the name of whoever signs the bill.

extras.label: Drawing the marks
extras.caption: Each mark at every circle size, with its line, its color token and where its parts sit. Read <surface> as “newsprint” or “charcoal”, the ground the tracker sits on.

extras.label: Numbered steps in a 600 px column on Charcoal
extras.caption: The wide form, as on a tablet or in a desktop article column, on Charcoal, with two of the bills. Each step’s name sits under its circle, the current step’s name is bold, and the marks turn to Newsprint and Dim Newsprint while the take-part disc keeps its red.

extras.label: The 18 utility icons
extras.caption: Every utility icon at its two sizes, with the word that goes beside it.

extras.label: A phone menu, live at 360 px
extras.caption: Menu opens the chapter’s contents over the page and holds focus until Close or the Escape key shuts it, and focus then returns to Menu. Each row’s chevron opens its list of rules.

extras.label: The three marks in their messages
extras.caption: Error, success and warning at true size, each with its words.
